LIGHTNING INFRASTRUCTURE

Core Lightning Issues Emergency Binary-Only Patch

Ungovernable reporting · Citing note 6ac790

Core Lightning told every node operator to shut down or restart with an offline flag, and left it there. Following an undisclosed vulnerability, maintainers took the extraordinary step of withholding source code while deploying pre-compiled executables.

Two days later a fix arrived as signed binaries only. No source. That comes in a fortnight. The reasoning is that publishing the diff hands attackers a map to unpatched nodes. Fair enough. But you can reverse engineer a closed binary too, so you slow the clock down without stopping anyone. What you do get is an open source project asking you to trust a binary. That precedent outlasts this bug.

The incident has provoked sharp debate across node operators regarding operational security trade-offs and trust assumptions in critical routing software.

EXCHANGE SURVEILLANCE

HTX Dust Transfers Freeze Accounts on Kraken

Ungovernable reporting · Citing note d29510

Between the 17th and the 24th of August, wallets tied to sanctioned exchange HTX sent roughly 12,000 dust transfers into Kraken user addresses. The uninvited micro-deposits triggered compliance locks across thousands of customer accounts.

The deposits tripped Kraken's AML controls and froze the accounts. Access has been restored, but Kraken still holds 4.2 million it considers tainted, and restored access is not the same as getting your money back.

Sending dust from an address you know is sanctioned costs an attacker close to nothing, even at current mempool rates. It can cost the victim their entire account. This is what coin control is for, and it is what leaving coins on an exchange can cost you.

BITCOIN PROTOCOL & CONSENSUS

BIP-110 Collapses at 2% While Quantum Signatures Land on Mainnet

Miners reject the year's fiercest soft-fork campaign by overwhelming margins, even as independent researchers demonstrate post-quantum transactions on mainnet using existing script opcodes.

Contra and Ungovernable reporting · Citing article 3eebb7 · Citing note 59383b

The loudest Bitcoin fight of the year ended with about 2% of miners signaling for it. After months of polarized community debate over transaction metadata and arbitrary payload restrictions, the proposal to enforce strict trial caps collapsed as mining pools decisively passed on signaling.

BIP-110 wanted to cap arbitrary data in transactions for a one year trial. Adam Back called it a downgrade. Michael Saylor published a hundred and ten reasons against it. The signaling window opened in August against a 55% early lock in threshold, and support sat at roughly 2%. Measured by volume it was a war. Measured by consensus it was a rounding error.

The failure highlights an enduring structural reality of Bitcoin governance: social volume does not translate into economic consensus. Yet while soft-fork activation mechanisms remain conservative, cryptographic progress continues unhindered on the live chain.

In block 964199, an unannounced mainnet broadcast proved that long-standing worries over post-quantum vulnerability can be tackled today without altering a single consensus rule:

Two Starkware researchers broadcast a quantum resistant Bitcoin transaction on mainnet, in block 964199, using hash based one time signatures built from script opcodes that already exist. No consensus change. No soft fork. Nobody had to ask Bitcoin Core for anything.

The transaction utilized Lamport-style hash-based one-time signatures constructed from existing Script operations, proving that forward-looking security upgrades do not require permission or contentious soft forks.

It is about five times the size of a normal transaction, so at fifty sats a byte it stings. At one sat a byte it is nothing. And if the alternative is being quantum vulnerable, that is a price worth paying. The headline is not the cost. It is that this was possible the whole time.

FREEDOM TECH WORKSHOP

Sovereign Engineering Funds Community Fab Lab

Sovereign Engineering reporting · Citing note 501a9f

Some participants come to Soveng carrying more than their laptops. They arrive with large backpacks and cases full of equipment to build.

Without a shared workshop or access to the right tools on the island, some builders could not do everything they had hoped to do. Builders at the cohort in Madeira organized to solve the bottleneck permanently, raising over three million satoshis for a shared fabrication lab.

What began with a couple of participants choosing to solve a problem has become a shared effort, with 3 million sats raised so far. The workshop, hosted at Nostr Office, equips developers with 3D printers, storage, and circuit analysis tools.

Veteran developer Johnathan Corgan observed of the gathering: The experience of Sovereign Engineering is transformative. It goes way beyond just "hacking on freedom tech". The combination of people, location, philosophy, and shared values is unlike anything I have been through before.

DEEP DISPATCHES

Analysis, Security & Protocol Releases

CYBERCRIME & SURVEILLANCE

153 Million Identity Records Leaked from Verification Gateway

Lyudmyla Kozlovska reporting · Citing note 5bc801

On Aug. 31, Brian Krebs reported that a new service on the Russian cybercrime forum Exploit was offering access to digital scans of identity documents on more than 153 million people in North America.

The breach compromised identity verification infrastructure serving major hospitality, logistics, and retail corporations, with customer data exfiltrated continuously over a twelve-month span prior to detection.

When 153 million identity documents sit in a single database for over a year, undetected, every person in that database becomes a potential target, not just for common fraud, but for transnational repression.

Advocates argued the catastrophe demonstrates that centralized identity aggregation mandates create dangerous attack surfaces that compromise civil liberties worldwide.

PROTOCOL RELEASES

Amber 6.6.1 Ships Permissions Hardening; ngit-grasp Debuts

greenart7c3 and DanConwayDev · Citing note 13aabb · Citing note 4f613a

Mobile signer Amber rolled out version 6.6.1, correcting permission list parsing when incoming JSON omitted kind tags and ensuring rejected signer requests return their request id so invoking client apps can cleanly handle declined signatures.

Simultaneously, code collaboration on Nostr advanced with the release of `ngit-grasp`, a Rust implementation of Git Relays Authorized via Signed-Nostr Proofs coupling decentralized repository state directly to Git Smart HTTP.

The dual releases illustrate the quiet hardening of signing and code review infrastructure across native client tooling.

P2P ESCROW

Mostro Charts State Transitions for Non-Custodial Swaps

Mostro reporting · Citing note 0a31c7

A Mostro 🧌 trade moves through a clear sequence: you create an order, someone takes it, sats lock into a hold invoice, you confirm the fiat arrived, and the invoice settles.

The peer-to-peer exchange published an exhaustive architecture map detailing order lifecycle states, hold invoice verification, and dispute resolution logic.

By enforcing escrow strictly through cryptographic hold invoices, counterparty risk is minimized without routing transactions through centralized custodian accounts.

FIELD & HEARTH

Evening bike ride with the wife and kids. On the way back the sun went down and the sky just went off over the water. We stopped and stood there in silence for a bit. Weird how a big orange sky shuts everybody up. Half the stuff I stress about wouldn't survive ten minutes next to this view. It's free, it shows up every night, and somehow it beats everything money buys. Life could be worse. Be happy with what you actually have.
